title: AI System Design Patterns
subtitle: The architectures behind AI products
summary: Surveys six core architecture patterns for AI products: basic chatbot, RAG, single agent, multi-agent system, workflow agent, and human-in-the-loop. For each pattern it lists key components, pros/cons, and best-fit use cases, then walks through real-world design examples like an enterprise chatbot, an AI coding assistant, and a document QA system.

concepts.name: Basic Chatbot
concepts.summary: The simplest pattern: user input goes to an LLM with a system prompt and conversation history, and a response comes back.
keyPoints: Best for general Q&A and simple conversations
Components: LLM, conversation history, system prompt
Simple, fast, low cost
Limited to the model's training data

concepts.name: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
concepts.summary: Grounds LLM responses in a knowledge base via document ingestion, embeddings, a vector store, and a retriever.
keyPoints: Best for knowledge-grounded enterprise Q&A
Components: chunking, embeddings, vector store, retriever, LLM with context
Grounded, up-to-date, reduces hallucinations
More complex pipeline to build and maintain

concepts.name: Single Agent
concepts.summary: An LLM given a goal, tools (APIs, DB, code, search), and memory that runs a thought-action-observation loop to complete tasks.
keyPoints: Best for task automation, tool use, decision making
Can take real actions via tools
Harder to control than a plain chatbot
Uses short- and long-term memory

concepts.name: Multi-Agent System
concepts.summary: An orchestrator coordinates specialized agents (e.g. researcher, analyst, coder) that share memory and communicate to solve complex problems.
keyPoints: Best for complex, multi-domain problems and specialization
Parallel expertise via specialized agents
More design and coordination effort, higher cost
Harder to debug than single-agent setups

concepts.name: Workflow Agent
concepts.summary: A deterministic DAG of steps (LLM calls or tools) with state management and guards/validators, ideal when reliability and compliance matter.
keyPoints: Best for deterministic business processes
Reliable, auditable, easier to validate
State/context managed explicitly across steps
Not ideal for open-ended tasks

concepts.name: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)
concepts.summary: Inserts human review and approval between the AI system's output and the final action for high-stakes decisions.
keyPoints: Best for high-stakes decisions and quality assurance
Adds audit trail and traceability
Enables learning from human feedback
Higher accuracy, ideal for sensitive domains

concepts.name: Common Building Blocks & Cross-Cutting Concerns
concepts.summary: All patterns share building blocks (LLM, prompt, memory, tools, observability) and cross-cutting concerns like security, privacy, safety, evaluation, monitoring, and cost control.
keyPoints: LLM, prompts/instructions, memory, tools and APIs
Observability and guardrails in every design
Evaluate quality, latency, and cost continuously

quickHits.question: How would you design an enterprise chatbot?
quickHits.answer: Use RAG plus human-in-the-loop. Ingest documents, embed and index them, then use hybrid search with reranking to retrieve context, and have the LLM answer with citations. Route high-risk answers through human review, and monitor quality, latency, and cost in production.

quickHits.question: How would you design an AI coding assistant?
quickHits.answer: Use an agent-plus-tools architecture. The agent understands the codebase (RAG over code), plans actions, and uses tools for reading/writing files, running the terminal, and executing tests. It iterates with a feedback loop and caches context for long sessions.

quickHits.question: When should you choose a workflow agent over a free-form agent?
quickHits.answer: Choose a workflow agent when the process is deterministic and must be reliable, auditable, or compliant — e.g. business process automation. A fixed DAG with guards and validators gives predictable behavior, while free-form agents suit open-ended tasks where flexibility outweighs control.

quickHits.question: What are the tradeoffs of a multi-agent system?
quickHits.answer: Multi-agent systems handle complex tasks better through specialization and parallel expertise, with an orchestrator coordinating agents like researcher, analyst, and coder. The cost is more design and coordination effort, higher token spend, and harder debugging, so use them only when a single agent genuinely can't handle the task.

quickHits.question: Why add human-in-the-loop to an AI system?
quickHits.answer: HITL adds a human review/approval step before actions or outputs take effect, which raises accuracy and accountability for high-stakes or sensitive decisions. It also provides an audit trail and generates feedback the system can learn from. The tradeoff is added latency and operational cost.

sourceText: AI SYSTEM DESIGN PATTERNS — The Architectures Behind AI Products. Every AI product is an architecture: choose the right pattern, scale it reliably, operate it in production. 1) Basic Chatbot: LLM + conversation history + system prompt; simple, fast, low cost; limited to training data. 2) RAG: knowledge base, ingestion & chunking, embeddings & vector store, retriever (vector/hybrid), LLM with retrieved context; grounded, up-to-date, reduces hallucinations; more complex. 3) Agent: goal, LLM, tools (API, DB, code, search), memory, thought-action-observation loop; can take actions; harder to control. 4) Multi-Agent: orchestrator/manager coordinating researcher/analyst/coder agents with shared or isolated memory; better for complex tasks; more coordination, higher cost, harder to debug. 5) Workflow Agent: DAG of steps with state management and guards/validators; reliable, deterministic, auditable; not for open-ended tasks. 6) HITL: human review/approval before action; higher accuracy, audit and traceability; ideal for sensitive domains. Common building blocks: LLM, prompt, memory, tools, observability & guardrails; cross-cutting: security, privacy, safety, evaluation, monitoring, cost. Examples: enterprise chatbot (RAG+HITL), AI coding assistant (agent+tools), document QA (RAG workflow with query rewrite, hybrid retrieval, rerank, citations). Key takeaway: the best AI systems are designed, not just prompted.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) on Azure
subtitle: How RAG works end-to-end with Azure AI Search and Azure OpenAI
summary: Walks through the end-to-end RAG process on Azure: ingest, prep and chunk, embed, store/index, retrieve, and generate, with an optional improvement loop. It maps each step to concrete Azure services (Blob Storage, Data Factory, Azure AI Search, Azure OpenAI, Azure Monitor), shows a worked user-question flow with citations, and lists best practices like smart chunking, reranking, and metadata filtering.

concepts.name: End-to-End RAG Pipeline
concepts.summary: Six stages: ingest data, prep and chunk documents, embed chunks, store vectors in an index, retrieve relevant chunks at query time, and generate a grounded answer, plus an optional improve loop.
keyPoints: Ingest from SharePoint, Blob, SQL, websites, files
Chunk into ~300-800 token pieces with metadata
Retrieve top-k chunks and augment the prompt
Log interactions and iterate on data, prompts, retrieval

concepts.name: Chunking & Metadata
concepts.summary: Documents are cleaned, split into manageable chunks, and tagged with metadata like source, date, and title so retrieval can filter and cite.
keyPoints: Chunk by token count or semantic boundaries
Avoid splitting meaning across chunks
Metadata enables filtering (author, doc type, date)
OCR (Azure Document Intelligence) handles PDFs/images

concepts.name: Embeddings & Vector Indexing
concepts.summary: Chunks are converted to vectors with Azure OpenAI embeddings (text-embedding-3-large/small) and stored in Azure AI Search using an HNSW index for efficient similarity search.
keyPoints: Embeddings put similar concepts close in vector space
HNSW enables efficient approximate nearest-neighbor search
Cosine similarity ranks relevance
Supports hybrid (vector + keyword) search

concepts.name: Retrieval & Reranking
concepts.summary: At query time the user question is embedded and the index returns top-k chunks with scores; a semantic ranker or cross-encoder can rerank for precision.
keyPoints: Query embedded the same way as documents
Top-k results returned with scores and metadata
Reranking improves precision over raw similarity

concepts.name: Grounded Generation with Citations
concepts.summary: Retrieved chunks are added to the prompt alongside system instructions and the user question, and the LLM generates an answer with source citations.
keyPoints: Prompt = system instructions + question + retrieved context
Instruct the model to use context only
Citations build trust and enable verification
Reduces hallucinations vs. ungrounded generation

concepts.name: Azure RAG Reference Stack
concepts.summary: A typical Azure RAG architecture: data sources feed an ingestion pipeline (Data Factory/indexers) into Azure AI Search, with Azure OpenAI for embeddings and generation, Key Vault for secrets, and Azure Monitor for logging.
keyPoints: Azure AI Search for vector index and hybrid search
Azure OpenAI Service for embeddings and LLMs
Azure Monitor/App Insights for tracing and quality
Key Vault for secrets and keys

quickHits.question: Why use RAG instead of fine-tuning for enterprise Q&A?
quickHits.answer: RAG grounds answers in your private, up-to-date data without retraining the model — you just update the index. It provides citations for verifiability, reduces hallucinations, and lets you enforce access control at retrieval time, which fine-tuning cannot easily do.

quickHits.question: Walk me through what happens when a user asks a question in a RAG system.
quickHits.answer: The question is embedded into a vector, the vector index (e.g. Azure AI Search) returns the top-k most similar chunks with scores and metadata, and those chunks are inserted into the prompt as context. The LLM then generates an answer grounded in that context and returns citations to the source documents.

quickHits.question: How do you choose a chunking strategy?
quickHits.answer: Chunk by token count (roughly 300-800 tokens) or by semantic boundaries like sections and paragraphs, taking care not to split meaning mid-thought. Attach metadata (source, date, title) to each chunk so retrieval can filter and answers can cite. The right size balances retrieval precision against context completeness.

quickHits.question: What is hybrid search and why use it?
quickHits.answer: Hybrid search combines vector similarity search with keyword (lexical) search, so you catch both semantic matches and exact terms like product names or IDs. Azure AI Search supports it natively, and adding a semantic reranker on top further improves precision of the final top-k results.

quickHits.question: How do you improve a RAG system after launch?
quickHits.answer: Log interactions and capture user feedback, then use monitoring (Azure Monitor/Application Insights) to trace queries and measure answer quality. Iterate on data freshness, chunking, retrieval strategy, reranking, and prompts. Evaluate faithfulness and relevance continuously rather than treating the pipeline as fixed.

sourceText: RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION (RAG): How it works on Azure. RAG combines your data with LLMs for accurate, up-to-date, domain-specific answers with citations. Benefits: grounded answers, uses private data, up-to-date without retraining, citations, fewer hallucinations. Process: 1) Ingest from SharePoint, Blob Storage, Azure SQL, Cosmos DB, websites/APIs, files. 2) Prep & Chunk: text extraction, remove noise, split into 300-800 token chunks, add metadata (source, date, title); OCR via Azure Document Intelligence. 3) Embed with Azure OpenAI embeddings (text-embedding-3-large/small). 4) Store in Azure AI Search vector index (HNSW), enabling hybrid vector+keyword search and filters. 5) Retrieve: embed the query, return top-k chunks with scores (cosine similarity), optionally rerank with semantic ranker. 6) Generate: prompt = system instructions + question + retrieved context; LLM answers with citations. 7) Improve: log, capture feedback, refine data/prompts/retrieval; monitor with Azure Monitor/App Insights. Example flow: HR question retrieves top 3 policy chunks (scores 0.92/0.88/0.83), answer cites sources. Best practices: high-quality data, smart chunking, metadata filters, reranking, context-only prompts, show citations, evaluate continuously. Use cases: enterprise search, IT helpdesk copilots, policy assistants, support bots, research, onboarding.

title: Prompt Engineering Patterns
subtitle: Programming without code: seven patterns for better LLM outputs
summary: Covers seven prompt engineering patterns — zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, ReAct, self-consistency, and self-reflection — with examples, when to use each, strengths, and limitations. Includes a comparison table of token cost vs. reliability, best practices, and common pitfalls like vague instructions and poor example selection.

concepts.name: Zero-Shot Prompting
concepts.summary: Ask the model to perform a task with no examples, relying on its pre-trained knowledge.
keyPoints: Best for simple, well-defined tasks
Fast, cheap, minimal tokens
May be inconsistent on complex or nuanced tasks

concepts.name: One-Shot and Few-Shot Prompting
concepts.summary: Provide one or several examples to teach the model the desired pattern, style, or output format.
keyPoints: One-shot guides style/format at low token cost
Few-shot (2-10 examples) improves accuracy on complex tasks
Example quality and order strongly influence output
Curate diverse, representative examples

concepts.name: Chain of Thought (CoT)
concepts.summary: Prompt the model to reason step by step, breaking complex problems into intermediate steps.
keyPoints: Best for math, logic, multi-hop QA, planning
Improves accuracy and transparency
Reduces errors and hallucinations by exposing reasoning

concepts.name: ReAct (Reason + Act)
concepts.summary: Interleave reasoning with actions: the model thinks, calls a tool or search, observes the result, and continues until it can answer.
keyPoints: Thought -> Action -> Observation loop
Best when tasks need tools, APIs, or real-time info
Produces grounded, up-to-date responses

concepts.name: Self-Consistency
concepts.summary: Sample multiple independent reasoning paths and take the majority-vote answer so errors in individual paths cancel out.
keyPoints: Best for hard reasoning and math problems
Higher accuracy without changing the model
Costs more tokens due to multiple samples

concepts.name: Self-Reflection
concepts.summary: A multi-stage pattern where the model answers, critiques its own output for gaps or errors, then produces an improved answer.
keyPoints: Stage 1 answer, stage 2 self-review, stage 3 improved answer
Best for high-stakes or long-form tasks
Improves accuracy, completeness, and clarity

concepts.name: Best Practices & Pitfalls
concepts.summary: Effective prompting is clear, structured, and iterated; common failures come from vagueness, poor examples, and ignoring output format.
keyPoints: Use delimiters to separate prompt parts
Provide only necessary context; watch token usage
Test edge cases and iterate on prompts
Don't rely on zero-shot for complex tasks

quickHits.question: When would you use few-shot prompting?
quickHits.answer: Use few-shot when the task is complex, requires a specific output format, or the model is inconsistent with zero-shot. A handful of curated examples teaches the pattern and improves accuracy, at the cost of extra tokens. Example quality and ordering matter a lot.

quickHits.question: What is ReAct?
quickHits.answer: ReAct (Reason + Act) is a pattern where the model reasons about a problem, takes an action using tools or APIs, observes the result, and continues reasoning iteratively until it produces a final answer. It's ideal for tasks needing search, calculation, or dynamic real-time information.

quickHits.question: How does chain-of-thought improve reasoning?
quickHits.answer: CoT prompts the model to break problems into intermediate steps rather than jumping to an answer. This exposes assumptions, reduces errors, improves accuracy on math and multi-hop questions, and makes the reasoning interpretable so you can spot where it went wrong.

quickHits.question: What is self-consistency and when is it worth the cost?
quickHits.answer: Self-consistency samples multiple reasoning paths for the same question and takes the majority-vote answer, since independent paths tend to cancel out individual errors. It raises accuracy on hard reasoning and math tasks without any model changes, but multiplies token cost, so reserve it for problems where correctness justifies the spend.

quickHits.question: Name common prompt engineering pitfalls.
quickHits.answer: Vague instructions, too many or low-quality examples, ignoring output format, overly long prompts that waste tokens, relying on zero-shot for complex tasks, and not testing edge cases. The fix is clear structured instructions, delimiters, curated examples, and iterative evaluation of prompts.

sourceText: PROMPT ENGINEERING PATTERNS — Programming Without Code. Patterns are high-leverage techniques for better, more reliable, controllable LLM outputs. 1) Zero-Shot: no examples; simple well-defined tasks; fast and cheap but inconsistent on complex tasks. 2) One-Shot: one example to guide style/format at low token cost; example quality drives output. 3) Few-Shot: multiple examples (2-10) teach the pattern; high accuracy for complex tasks/formats; higher token cost, sensitive to example selection and order. 4) Chain of Thought: 'think step by step'; breaks problems into intermediate steps; best for math, logic, multi-hop QA, planning; improves accuracy, transparency, fewer hallucinations. 5) ReAct (Reason+Act): thought -> action (tool/search) -> observation loop; for tool use, APIs, dynamic info; grounded, up-to-date answers. 6) Self-Consistency: sample multiple reasoning paths, majority vote; errors cancel out; higher accuracy without changing the model; high sample cost. 7) Self-Reflection: answer, self-review for issues, improved answer; for high-stakes/long-form tasks. Comparison: token cost rises from zero-shot (very low) to self-reflection (high rounds); reliability rises correspondingly. Best practices: clear specific structured prompts, delimiters, minimal necessary context, iterate and evaluate, watch tokens. Pitfalls: vague instructions, poor examples, ignoring format, overlong prompts, zero-shot for complex tasks, untested edge cases. Takeaway: match the pattern to the task.
