title: Transformers & Attention
subtitle: The foundation of modern NLP
summary: Covers the transformer architecture that powers BERT, GPT, and T5: encoder-decoder structure, scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding, feed-forward layers, and masked self-attention for autoregressive decoding. Also compares complexity against RNNs and lists applications from translation to code generation.

concepts.name: Why Transformers
concepts.summary: Transformers replace recurrence and convolution with attention, capturing long-range dependencies while being highly parallelizable.
keyPoints: No vanishing-gradient problem for long-range dependencies
All positions processed in parallel, so training is fast
State-of-the-art across NLP, vision, and speech
Scales well with data and model size

concepts.name: Encoder-Decoder Architecture
concepts.summary: The encoder builds an understanding of the input sequence; the decoder generates output autoregressively, with attention layers at the core of both.
keyPoints: Encoder-only models like BERT excel at understanding tasks
Decoder-only models like GPT generate text autoregressively
Blocks combine attention, feed-forward networks, residual connections, and LayerNorm
Decoder uses cross-attention over encoder outputs in seq2seq models

concepts.name: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
concepts.summary: Attention computes softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k))V — a weighted sum of Values based on Query-Key similarity.
keyPoints: Q, K, V matrices are learned projections of the input
Scores are scaled by sqrt(d_k) to prevent large dot products and stabilize gradients
Softmax normalizes each row of scores to sum to 1

concepts.name: Multi-Head Attention
concepts.summary: Runs h attention heads in parallel, then concatenates and linearly projects their outputs.
keyPoints: Each head can attend to different positions
Heads capture different types of relationships in different subspaces
Produces more expressive representations than a single head

concepts.name: Positional Encoding
concepts.summary: Since transformers have no recurrence, sinusoidal position signals are added to token embeddings so the model knows token order.
keyPoints: PE uses sin/cos functions of position at different frequencies
Added directly to token embeddings
Sinusoidal form helps generalize to longer sequences

concepts.name: Masked Self-Attention
concepts.summary: In decoders, a causal mask prevents positions from attending to future tokens, enabling autoregressive generation.
keyPoints: Each position can attend only to itself and earlier positions
Prevents 'peeking' at future tokens during training
Used in GPT-style models for both training and inference

concepts.name: Complexity vs RNNs
concepts.summary: Self-attention is O(n^2) in sequence length but fully parallel, while RNNs are sequential and struggle with long-range dependencies.
keyPoints: Attention lets all positions interact in one step
RNNs require sequential steps and are hard to parallelize
For very long sequences, sparse or linear attention variants reduce cost

quickHits.question: What is the core idea of transformers?
quickHits.answer: Transformers replace recurrence and convolution with attention mechanisms to model relationships between all positions in a sequence directly. This lets the model capture long-range dependencies in a single step and process every position in parallel, which makes training dramatically faster and more scalable than RNNs.

quickHits.question: Why is the attention score scaled by sqrt(d_k)?
quickHits.answer: For large key dimensions, raw dot products grow in magnitude, pushing the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps the scores in a reasonable range, stabilizing gradients and making training well-behaved.

quickHits.question: What is the difference between the encoder and the decoder?
quickHits.answer: The encoder reads the entire input sequence bidirectionally to build contextual representations — it understands the input. The decoder generates output tokens one at a time autoregressively, using masked self-attention over what it has generated so far and (in seq2seq models) cross-attention over the encoder's outputs. BERT is encoder-only; GPT is decoder-only.

quickHits.question: What does multi-head attention buy you over a single head?
quickHits.answer: Each head projects Q, K, and V into a different subspace, so different heads can attend to different positions and capture different types of relationships — for example syntax in one head and coreference in another. Concatenating and projecting the heads yields richer, more expressive representations than a single attention function.

quickHits.question: Why do transformers need positional encoding?
quickHits.answer: Self-attention is permutation-invariant — it has no built-in notion of token order because there is no recurrence or convolution. Positional encodings (e.g., sinusoidal signals added to the embeddings) inject order information so the model can distinguish 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'. Sinusoidal encodings also allow some generalization to sequence lengths not seen in training.

quickHits.question: What is the complexity of self-attention and how do you handle long sequences?
quickHits.answer: Self-attention is O(n^2) in sequence length for both compute and memory, since every token attends to every other token. It is highly parallelizable, so it is fast on modern hardware for moderate lengths, but for very long sequences you use sparse, linear, or windowed attention variants to reduce the quadratic cost.

sourceText: Transformers & Attention — The Foundation of Modern NLP. Transformers rely on attention instead of recurrence or convolution and power BERT, GPT, T5. Why: capture long-range dependencies without vanishing gradients, highly parallelizable, state-of-the-art across NLP/CV/speech, scalable. Architecture: token embeddings + positional encoding feed encoder (understands input) and decoder (generates output autoregressively); blocks use multi-head self-attention, cross-attention (decoder), feed-forward networks, residual Add & Norm. Scaled dot-product attention: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V — a weighted sum of Values by Query-Key similarity; scaling prevents large dot products and stabilizes gradients. Multi-head attention: h parallel heads, concat + linear projection; attends to different positions and relationship types in different subspaces. Positional encoding: sinusoidal PE(pos) with sin/cos added to embeddings; generalizes to longer sequences. Position-wise FFN: Linear -> ReLU/GELU -> Linear, adds non-linearity and capacity. Masked self-attention prevents attending to future tokens for autoregressive generation. Complexity: RNNs are sequential and hard to parallelize; attention is parallel with better long-range modeling; use sparse/linear attention for very long sequences. Uses: translation, language modeling, classification, QA, summarization, code generation, multimodal.

title: AI Latency Optimization
subtitle: Making AI feel instant
summary: A playbook of six techniques for cutting latency in AI/LLM applications: streaming responses, parallel retrieval, async tool calls, caching, right-sized model selection, and retrieval optimization. Shows how the techniques compose into an optimized pipeline delivering roughly 50-80% lower latency and 30-70% lower cost, and lists common pitfalls.

concepts.name: Streaming Responses
concepts.summary: Send tokens to the user as they are generated instead of waiting for the full response, drastically improving perceived latency.
keyPoints: Perceived latency drops from seconds to sub-second even if total time is similar
Stream by default for chat and long responses
Show typing indicators to set expectations

concepts.name: Parallel Retrieval
concepts.summary: Run vector search, keyword search, and other retrieval steps concurrently rather than sequentially.
keyPoints: Sequential vector DB -> keyword -> re-rank took 2.1s; parallel took 1.1s (~48% faster)
Use hybrid search combined with re-ranking
Re-rank only after parallel candidate retrieval completes

concepts.name: Async Tool Calls
concepts.summary: Execute independent tool calls concurrently instead of one after another.
keyPoints: Three sequential tools totaling 4.0s ran in ~1.2s concurrently (~70% faster)
Only parallelize tools with no data dependencies
Set timeouts and fallbacks for slow tools

concepts.name: Caching
concepts.summary: Cache expensive, reused work: semantic prompt/response caches, embeddings, retrieval results, and stable tool responses.
keyPoints: Semantic caching avoids re-generating similar answers
Cache embeddings to avoid re-embedding the same text
Use TTLs and cache invalidation; semantic cache beats exact-match cache

concepts.name: Model Selection and Routing
concepts.summary: Use the smallest model that gets the job done, routing by task complexity rather than hype.
keyPoints: Simple Q&A: small models (e.g., gpt-4o-mini, llama-3.1-8b)
Complex reasoning: escalate to stronger models only when needed
Smaller models mean lower latency, lower cost, higher throughput

concepts.name: Retrieval Optimization
concepts.summary: Retrieve less but smarter: better chunking, metadata filtering, top-k tuning, and late re-ranking.
keyPoints: Use smaller meaningful chunks (200-500 tokens)
Filter by metadata before vector search
Top-k of ~3-8 is often enough; re-rank only top candidates with a cross-encoder

concepts.name: Composed Optimized Pipeline
concepts.summary: Cache check -> parallel retrieval -> re-rank -> LLM with streaming and async tools compounds the gains.
keyPoints: Example end-to-end: 7.2s unoptimized down to 3.8s optimized
Total impact: 50-80% lower latency, 30-70% lower cost
Measure end-to-end latency, then optimize, monitor, iterate

quickHits.question: How would you reduce latency in an LLM chatbot?
quickHits.answer: Attack the whole pipeline: stream responses so users see tokens immediately, run retrieval searches in parallel, execute independent tool calls asynchronously, and cache aggressively (semantic response cache, embeddings, retrieval results). Route simple requests to smaller, faster models and reserve large models for complex reasoning. Finally, optimize retrieval itself — smaller chunks, metadata filtering, and modest top-k — and measure end-to-end latency continuously.

quickHits.question: Why does streaming matter if total generation time is unchanged?
quickHits.answer: Streaming transforms perceived performance: users see the first tokens in a few hundred milliseconds instead of staring at a spinner for several seconds. It keeps users engaged, hides model generation time, and is especially valuable for long responses. Perceived latency drives user satisfaction as much as actual latency.

quickHits.question: When should you use a smaller model instead of the biggest one?
quickHits.answer: Use smaller models when the task is simple (extraction, classification, straightforward Q&A, summarization), when latency or cost is critical, or when volume is high. With clear guardrails and good context, small models handle most traffic well. A router can escalate to a larger model when confidence is low, giving you big-model quality only where it is needed.

quickHits.question: What should you cache in a RAG system?
quickHits.answer: Cache the expensive, reusable pieces: prompt/response pairs via a semantic cache to skip regeneration of similar answers, embeddings so identical text is never re-embedded, retrieval results for repeated or similar queries, and stable tool/API responses. Use TTLs and explicit invalidation so cached data does not go stale, and prefer semantic matching over exact-match keys.

quickHits.question: What are common latency pitfalls in AI systems?
quickHits.answer: Typical mistakes include not streaming long responses, running retrieval and tool calls sequentially, having no caching strategy, using large models for trivially simple tasks, retrieving far too much context, and ignoring timeouts and fallbacks. The meta-pitfall is not measuring end-to-end latency at all — you cannot optimize what you do not measure.

sourceText: AI Latency Optimization — Making AI Feel Instant. Lower latency improves UX, engagement, and adoption. 1) Streaming responses: send tokens as generated; perceived latency drops to ~0.6s vs 4.2s; stream by default, show typing indicators. 2) Parallel retrieval: run vector + keyword searches concurrently then re-rank; 2.1s sequential -> 1.1s parallel (~48% faster); use hybrid search + re-rank. 3) Async tool calls: run independent tools concurrently; 4.0s sequential -> ~1.2s (~70% faster); set timeouts and fallbacks. 4) Caching: semantic prompt/response cache, embeddings, retrieval results, stable tool responses; use TTL and invalidation; semantic > exact match. 5) Model selection: smallest model that does the job — small models for simple Q&A, mid models for general chat, strong models for complex reasoning; route cheap first, escalate when needed. 6) Retrieval optimization: 200-500 token chunks, metadata filtering before vector search, top-k ~3-8, cross-encoder re-rank on top results. Combined pipeline (cache check -> parallel retrieval -> re-rank -> LLM streaming + async tools): 50-80% lower latency, 30-70% lower cost; example 7.2s -> 3.8s end-to-end. Pitfalls: no streaming, sequential calls, no caching, oversized models, too much context, no timeouts, not measuring. Measure -> Optimize -> Monitor -> Iterate.

title: Overfitting vs. Underfitting
subtitle: Can the model generalize?
summary: Explains the spectrum from underfitting (too simple, high bias) through good fit to overfitting (too complex, high variance) using studying-for-a-test and dartboard analogies. Covers the training-vs-validation error curve, the three main knobs (model complexity, data amount, regularization), signs of overfitting, and standard fixes for each failure mode.

concepts.name: Underfit vs Good Fit vs Overfit
concepts.summary: An underfit model is too simple and misses obvious patterns; an overfit model is too complex and captures noise; a good fit captures the true pattern.
keyPoints: Underfitting = high bias, model knows too little
Overfitting = high variance, model memorizes training data including noise
Analogy: didn't study vs learned concepts vs memorized the answer key

concepts.name: Training vs Validation Error Curve
concepts.summary: As complexity grows, training error keeps falling while validation error falls then rises; the best model sits at the validation minimum.
keyPoints: Underfit region: both training and validation error are high
Overfit region: low training error but much higher validation error
Pick the complexity where validation error is lowest

concepts.name: The Three Knobs
concepts.summary: Model complexity, amount of data, and regularization strength are the primary levers controlling the bias-variance tradeoff.
keyPoints: More complexity: lower bias but higher variance and overfit risk
More data: better generalization, lower overfit risk
Stronger regularization: less flexibility, lower overfit risk

concepts.name: Signs of Overfitting
concepts.summary: A large gap between training and validation performance is the classic symptom.
keyPoints: Training accuracy extremely high while validation is much lower
Performance drops in production
Model is sensitive to small changes in data or hyperparameters

concepts.name: Fixes for Each Failure Mode
concepts.summary: Underfitting and overfitting have opposite remedies.
keyPoints: Underfitting: bigger model, more features, train longer, reduce regularization
Overfitting: more data, simpler model, L1/L2 regularization, dropout, early stopping

concepts.name: Diagnosis Decision Framework
concepts.summary: Compare training and validation errors to classify the problem.
keyPoints: High training error: underfit (high bias)
Low training error but much higher validation error: overfit (high variance)
Low training error and similar validation error: good model

quickHits.question: What is the difference between overfitting and underfitting?
quickHits.answer: Underfitting means the model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern — it has high bias and performs poorly even on training data. Overfitting means the model is too complex and memorizes the training data, including noise — it has high variance, so training performance is excellent but validation and production performance are much worse. The goal is a good fit that captures the true signal and generalizes to unseen data.

quickHits.question: How do you detect overfitting?
quickHits.answer: Look at the gap between training and validation metrics: very high training accuracy with substantially lower validation accuracy is the classic signature. Other signs include performance degrading in production relative to offline results and high sensitivity to small changes in data or hyperparameters. Plotting training vs validation error against model complexity or epochs makes the divergence visible.

quickHits.question: How would you fix an overfitting model?
quickHits.answer: Reduce variance: get more training data, simplify the model, add L1/L2 regularization, use dropout, or apply early stopping. Data augmentation and feature reduction also help. Each of these constrains the model's ability to memorize noise, trading a bit of training accuracy for better generalization.

quickHits.question: How would you fix an underfitting model?
quickHits.answer: Increase capacity and signal: use a bigger or more expressive model, add more informative features, train longer, or reduce regularization strength. Underfitting is a high-bias problem, so the remedies all involve letting the model learn more from the data rather than constraining it further.

quickHits.question: How does the bias-variance tradeoff relate to model complexity?
quickHits.answer: As complexity increases, bias decreases because the model can represent richer patterns, but variance increases because it becomes more sensitive to the specific training sample. Training error decreases monotonically with complexity, while validation error is U-shaped. The optimal complexity is at the bottom of the validation-error curve, where the sum of bias and variance effects is minimized.

sourceText: Overfitting vs. Underfitting — Can the Model Generalize? Underfit: too simple, misses obvious patterns (high bias). Good fit: captures the true pattern. Overfit: too complex, captures signal + noise (high variance). Studying analogy: didn't study (underfit), learned concepts (good), memorized the answer key (overfit — fails on new questions). Training error falls with complexity; validation error is U-shaped — the best model is where validation error is lowest. Three knobs: 1) Model complexity — more complexity lowers bias but raises variance and overfit risk; 2) Amount of data — more data improves generalization and lowers overfit risk; 3) Regularization — stronger regularization reduces flexibility and overfit risk. House price example: underfit rule 'every house costs $300k' gives huge errors; good fit uses meaningful features (bedrooms, bathrooms, square feet); overfit memorizes 'blue mailbox + oak tree = $412,937' and fails on new houses. Overfitting signs: very high training accuracy, much lower validation accuracy, production drops, sensitivity to small changes. Fixes — underfitting: bigger model, more features, train longer, less regularization; overfitting: more data, simpler model, L1/L2, dropout, early stopping. Dartboard analogy: underfit misses badly, good fit hits center consistently, overfit hits the training board but misses the new target. Generalization is the goal.

title: Cross-Validation (CV)
subtitle: Better models, smarter evaluation
summary: Explains why a single train/test split can give a lucky or unlucky performance estimate and how k-fold cross-validation produces a more reliable one by rotating the validation fold and averaging scores. Covers k-fold, stratified k-fold, and leave-one-out variants, pros and cons, best practices, and pitfalls like data leakage and tuning on the test set.

concepts.name: Why Cross-Validation
concepts.summary: A single train/test split has high variance — the score depends on how the data happened to be split; CV averages over multiple splits for a stable estimate.
keyPoints: Single split can be lucky or unlucky
CV gives a more stable, trustworthy evaluation
Every data point is used for both training and validation exactly once

concepts.name: k-Fold Mechanics
concepts.summary: Split data into k equal folds; train on k-1 folds and validate on the remaining one, rotating k times, then average the scores.
keyPoints: k = 5 or 10 is the common default
Final score = average of the k validation scores
More folds give a more stable estimate at higher compute cost

concepts.name: CV Variants
concepts.summary: Different strategies fit different data: standard k-fold, stratified k-fold, and leave-one-out.
keyPoints: Stratified k-fold preserves class distribution in each fold — best for imbalanced classification
Leave-one-out uses k = n, training on n-1 samples each time
Time-series data needs time-aware splits, not shuffled CV

concepts.name: When to Use CV
concepts.summary: CV shines for model comparison, small datasets, and reducing split variance; it is overkill for extremely large datasets.
keyPoints: Compare algorithms or hyperparameters fairly
Make the most of limited data
For huge datasets, a simple holdout or time-based split is fine

concepts.name: Pros and Cons
concepts.summary: CV is more reliable than a single split but more expensive and still needs care.
keyPoints: Pros: uses all data, lower variance, better for tuning
Cons: computationally expensive, can be biased for time series, leakage risk
Results can vary with the choice of k

concepts.name: Pitfalls and Best Practices
concepts.summary: Leakage, wrong k, imbalanced folds, and tuning on the test set undermine CV estimates.
keyPoints: Fit preprocessing inside each fold to avoid leakage
Shuffle before splitting unless data is time-ordered
Tune with CV, then evaluate once on an untouched holdout test set
Report mean and standard deviation of CV scores

quickHits.question: Why use cross-validation instead of a single train/test split?
quickHits.answer: A single split gives a high-variance estimate — the score depends on which examples happened to land in the test set. Cross-validation trains and validates on multiple rotated splits and averages the scores, producing a more stable and trustworthy estimate of generalization. It also uses every data point for both training and validation, which matters most with limited data.

quickHits.question: How does k-fold cross-validation work?
quickHits.answer: Split the data into k equal folds. For each of k iterations, train on k-1 folds and validate on the held-out fold, rotating which fold is held out. The final CV score is the average of the k validation scores, often reported with its standard deviation. k = 5 or 10 balances reliability against compute cost.

quickHits.question: When would you use stratified k-fold?
quickHits.answer: For classification with imbalanced classes. Stratified k-fold preserves the overall class distribution within each fold, so every fold is representative. Without stratification, some folds might contain very few minority-class examples, skewing both training and the validation scores.

quickHits.question: How can data leakage happen during cross-validation?
quickHits.answer: The most common way is fitting preprocessing — scaling, imputation, feature selection, target encoding — on the full dataset before splitting, so information from validation folds leaks into training. The fix is to run the entire pipeline inside each fold, for example with sklearn's Pipeline inside cross_val_score. Leakage inflates CV scores and produces models that disappoint in production.

quickHits.question: Does cross-validation replace the test set?
quickHits.answer: No. CV is for model selection and hyperparameter tuning; once you have repeatedly used CV scores to make decisions, they become optimistically biased. You should still keep a completely untouched holdout test set and evaluate on it exactly once at the end for an honest final estimate.

quickHits.question: What are the tradeoffs in choosing k?
quickHits.answer: Small k (e.g., 3) is cheap but gives higher-variance estimates and trains on less data per fold. Large k approaches leave-one-out: low bias but very expensive and the estimates across folds are highly correlated. k = 5 or 10 is the standard compromise between reliability and compute.

sourceText: Cross-Validation (CV) — Better Models, Smarter Evaluation. Problem: a single train/test split can give a lucky or unlucky estimate with high variance; CV uses multiple splits for reliable evaluation. k-Fold: split into k equal folds, train on k-1, validate on 1, rotate k times, average the k scores; every data point is used for training and validation exactly once; more folds = more stable estimate but higher compute. Variants: k-fold (k=5 or 10 common), stratified k-fold (preserves class distribution, best for imbalanced classification), leave-one-out (k=n). When to use: model comparison, small datasets, unstable splits, reliable estimates; not ideal for extremely large datasets (use holdout or time-based split). Pros: uses all data, more reliable than single split, lower variance, better for tuning. Cons: computationally expensive, can be biased for time series, leakage risk, results vary with k. Best practices: shuffle before splitting (unless time-ordered), stratify for imbalance, tune with CV then evaluate on an untouched holdout test set, report mean and std of scores. Pitfalls: data leakage from validation fold into training, wrong k (too small = high variance, too large = high cost), imbalanced folds, tuning on the test set. Mnemonic RELIABLE: Repeat, Evaluate, Leverage, Improve, Aggregate, Balance, Learn, Estimate.

title: Hyperparameter Tuning
subtitle: Find the best settings, get the best model
summary: Covers what hyperparameters are and why they must be set before training, then compares tuning methods: grid search, random search, Bayesian optimization, and Hyperband/ASHA. Walks through a random forest grid-search example, the tuning workflow, best practices like using k-fold CV and experiment tracking, and pitfalls such as data leakage and overfitting to the validation set.

concepts.name: What Hyperparameters Are
concepts.summary: Hyperparameters control how a model learns and are set before training rather than learned from data.
keyPoints: Examples: learning rate, number of trees, max depth, regularization, batch size
Good choices improve performance and generalization
Bad choices cause underfitting or overfitting

concepts.name: Tuning as Search
concepts.summary: Tuning is a search problem: define a search space, try combinations, evaluate on validation data, and pick the best.
keyPoints: 1. Define search space (ranges or values)
2. Train models with different settings
3. Score each with a validation metric
4. Select the best-scoring configuration

concepts.name: Grid Search vs Random Search
concepts.summary: Grid search exhaustively tries every combination; random search samples the space and is usually more efficient in high dimensions.
keyPoints: Grid: simple but cost explodes as dimensions grow (e.g., 3x4x3x2 = 72 combos)
Random: covers more values per dimension for the same budget
Random search is a strong default starting point

concepts.name: Bayesian Optimization and Hyperband/ASHA
concepts.summary: Advanced methods use past results or early stopping of poor configs to search more efficiently.
keyPoints: Bayesian optimization models the score surface and picks promising points
Hyperband/ASHA allocate more resources to promising configurations
Great for expensive deep-learning training runs

concepts.name: Tuning Workflow
concepts.summary: A disciplined loop: define the problem and metric, choose a search method and space, run the search, analyze results, then validate and test.
keyPoints: Tune for the metric that matters to the problem
Search space size and compute budget bound how thorough you can be
Confirm the final choice on a held-out test set before deploying

concepts.name: Best Practices and Pitfalls
concepts.summary: Sound evaluation discipline matters as much as the search algorithm.
keyPoints: Use k-fold CV for robust scoring and track all experiments
Avoid data leakage — never touch the test set during tuning
Beware overfitting to the validation set: best val score may not be best test score
Search space too small misses optima; too large wastes compute

quickHits.question: What is the difference between parameters and hyperparameters?
quickHits.answer: Parameters (weights, tree split thresholds) are learned from data during training. Hyperparameters — learning rate, max depth, number of trees, regularization strength, batch size — control how learning happens and must be set before training. Since they are not learned, we find good values by searching and evaluating on validation data.

quickHits.question: Grid search vs random search — which would you pick and why?
quickHits.answer: Random search is usually the better default. Grid search cost grows multiplicatively with each dimension and wastes budget on unimportant hyperparameters, while random search explores more distinct values per important dimension for the same number of trials. Grid search is fine for a small, low-dimensional, well-understood space.

quickHits.question: How does Bayesian optimization work for hyperparameter tuning?
quickHits.answer: It builds a probabilistic surrogate model (often a Gaussian process or tree-based model) of the validation score as a function of the hyperparameters, then uses an acquisition function to choose the next configuration that balances exploring uncertain regions with exploiting promising ones. Because each choice is informed by past results, it typically finds good configurations in far fewer trials than grid or random search — valuable when each training run is expensive.

quickHits.question: How do you avoid overfitting to the validation set while tuning?
quickHits.answer: Use k-fold cross-validation rather than a single validation split so scores are stable, limit the number of configurations judged against the same data, and keep a completely untouched test set for the final check. The best validation score does not guarantee the best test score, so always revalidate the winning configuration on unseen data before deploying.

quickHits.question: What is Hyperband/ASHA and when is it useful?
quickHits.answer: Hyperband and ASHA are early-stopping-based methods: they start many configurations with small budgets (few epochs or samples), then progressively allocate more resources only to the promising ones. This makes them very efficient for deep learning, where full training runs are expensive and bad configurations can be identified early.

sourceText: Hyperparameter Tuning — Find the Best Settings, Get the Best Model. Hyperparameters (learning rate, number of trees, max depth, regularization, batch size) control how a model learns; they are not learned from data and must be set before training. Good choices improve performance; bad choices cause under/overfitting. Core loop: define search space -> try combinations -> evaluate with a validation score -> choose the best. Methods: Grid Search (every combination; simple but expensive as dimensions grow — e.g., 3x4x3x2 = 72 combos for a random forest over n_estimators, max_depth, min_samples_split, max_features), Random Search (samples combinations; more efficient, strong default), Bayesian Optimization (model-based smart search using past results; very efficient but more complex), Hyperband/ASHA (allocate more resources to promising configs; great for deep learning). Tuning is affected by search space size, compute budget, data amount, and metric choice. Workflow: define problem/metric -> choose search method and space -> run search -> analyze results -> validate and test, then deploy. Best practices: start with a baseline, default to random search, use k-fold CV, tune one model at a time, track experiments. Pitfalls: too small or too large search space, data leakage (using test data during tuning), inconsistent evaluation, overfitting to the validation set — best val score is not always best test score. Always confirm on an unseen test set.

title: Regularization
subtitle: Prevent overfitting. Improve generalization.
summary: Explains why complex models overfit by memorizing noise and how regularization adds a complexity penalty to improve generalization. Covers L1 (Lasso), L2 (Ridge), dropout, early stopping, weight decay, and data augmentation, plus how to tune the regularization strength lambda with cross-validation and common pitfalls of over- or under-regularizing.

concepts.name: Why Regularize
concepts.summary: Complex models can fit training data too closely, memorizing noise instead of signal, leading to high variance and poor performance on unseen data.
keyPoints: Underfit = too simple, high bias
Overfit = too complex, high variance
Goal: flexible but not too flexible
Penalty on complexity keeps models honest

concepts.name: L2 Regularization (Ridge)
concepts.summary: Adds the sum of squared weights to the loss, shrinking large weights toward zero without eliminating them.
keyPoints: Loss = MSE + lambda * sum(theta^2)
Shrinks weights smoothly
Equivalent to weight decay in neural nets
Keeps all features, just smaller

concepts.name: L1 Regularization (Lasso)
concepts.summary: Adds the sum of absolute weights to the loss, which can drive some weights exactly to zero and produce sparse models.
keyPoints: Loss = MSE + lambda * sum(|theta|)
Encourages sparsity
Acts as built-in feature selection
Corner solutions zero out weights

concepts.name: Dropout
concepts.summary: Randomly drops neurons during training so the network cannot rely on any single unit, preventing co-adaptation.
keyPoints: Applied only at training time
Prevents co-adaptation of neurons
Simple and effective for deep nets

concepts.name: Early Stopping
concepts.summary: Stop training when validation error starts rising even though training error keeps falling.
keyPoints: Monitor validation loss each epoch
Stop at the validation minimum
Cheap, implicit regularization

concepts.name: Tuning Lambda
concepts.summary: The regularization strength controls the bias-variance tradeoff; cross-validation finds the sweet spot between overfitting and underfitting.
keyPoints: Small lambda: low bias, high variance (overfit)
Large lambda: high bias, low variance (underfit)
Best lambda = lowest validation error
Sweep lambda on a log scale

quickHits.question: What is the difference between L1 and L2 regularization?
quickHits.answer: L2 penalizes squared weights, shrinking them smoothly toward zero but rarely to exactly zero; L1 penalizes absolute weights and can set some weights exactly to zero, yielding sparse models. Use L1 when you want implicit feature selection, L2 when you want stable shrinkage of all coefficients. L2 is also equivalent to weight decay in gradient-based training.

quickHits.question: How does regularization affect the bias-variance tradeoff?
quickHits.answer: Increasing regularization strength raises bias and lowers variance, while too little regularization leaves variance high and risks overfitting. The optimal strength minimizes validation error, balancing training fit against generalization. Cross-validation over a range of lambda values is the standard way to find that sweet spot.

quickHits.question: Why does dropout help a neural network generalize?
quickHits.answer: Dropout randomly zeroes out neurons during training, so the network cannot depend on specific units co-adapting. This forces redundant, robust representations and acts like training an ensemble of subnetworks. At inference, all units are active with scaled weights, giving an averaged prediction.

quickHits.question: How is early stopping a form of regularization?
quickHits.answer: Training error keeps decreasing, but validation error typically forms a U-shape; stopping at the validation minimum prevents the model from fitting noise in later epochs. It effectively limits the model's capacity to overfit without changing the loss function, and it costs almost nothing to implement.

quickHits.question: How would you choose the regularization strength lambda?
quickHits.answer: Sweep lambda across a log scale and evaluate each value with cross-validation, picking the one with the lowest validation error. Small lambda overfits (low bias, high variance) and large lambda underfits (high bias, low variance). Monitor the train-versus-validation gap and re-tune as data or features change.

sourceText: Regularization: prevent overfitting, improve generalization by adding a penalty for complexity. Problem: complex models fit training data too closely and memorize noise (underfit = high bias/too simple; overfit = high variance/too complex). Techniques: L2 (Ridge) penalizes large weights, J = MSE + lambda*sum(theta^2), shrinks weights; L1 (Lasso) J = MSE + lambda*sum(|theta|), encourages sparsity (weights exactly zero). Other methods: Dropout (randomly drops neurons, prevents co-adaptation), Early Stopping (stop before overfitting when val error rises), Weight Decay (equivalent to L2), Data Augmentation (more diverse training data). Effect: fit the data + penalize complexity = generalize better. Choosing lambda: use cross-validation; small lambda = overfitting, large lambda = underfitting, best lambda = lowest validation error. Practical guidelines: start simple, add regularization when overfitting appears, tune lambda by CV, monitor train vs validation. Pitfalls: too little (memorizes noise), too much (underfits), wrong type (L1 vs L2 vs dropout work differently), ignoring data/features/tuning. Memory: the 3 R's - Reduce complexity, Regularize smartly, Reach better generalization. Regularize to generalize.

title: Loss Functions
subtitle: Measuring error. Guiding learning.
summary: Introduces loss functions as the mechanism that turns prediction errors into a single number a model can minimize. Compares MSE and MAE for regression with binary and categorical cross-entropy for classification, shows how outliers affect each, and explains how loss drives weight updates via gradient descent along with common mistakes like using the wrong loss or ignoring validation loss.

concepts.name: What a Loss Function Does
concepts.summary: A loss function compares predictions to true values, converts the difference into a number, aggregates over examples, and provides the feedback signal for parameter updates.
keyPoints: Lower loss = better predictions
Training = minimizing loss
Loss is the model's compass

concepts.name: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
concepts.summary: Regression loss that averages squared errors, penalizing large errors much more heavily than small ones.
keyPoints: Quadratic penalty on error
Sensitive to outliers
Standard choice for continuous targets

concepts.name: Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
concepts.summary: Regression loss that averages absolute errors, treating all errors linearly and remaining robust to outliers.
keyPoints: Linear penalty on error
Robust to outliers
Prefer when data has extreme values

concepts.name: Binary Cross-Entropy (Log Loss)
concepts.summary: Classification loss for two-class problems that heavily penalizes confident wrong probability predictions.
keyPoints: Used for 0/1 targets
Loss = -[y log(p) + (1-y) log(1-p)]
Confident wrong answers cost the most

concepts.name: Categorical Cross-Entropy
concepts.summary: Multi-class classification loss over one-hot labels, comparing the predicted probability distribution to the true class.
keyPoints: Used with softmax outputs
One-hot encoded labels
Standard for image/text classification

concepts.name: Loss Drives Learning
concepts.summary: Gradient descent uses the loss to update weights step by step, moving the model from high loss (poor predictions) to low loss (better predictions).
keyPoints: Compute loss, then update weights
Monitor train AND validation loss
Train loss down + val loss up = overfitting

quickHits.question: When would you prefer MAE over MSE for regression?
quickHits.answer: MAE penalizes errors linearly, so outliers have a bounded, proportional influence, whereas MSE squares errors and lets a few extreme points dominate the loss. If your data contains outliers or heavy tails, MAE (or a robust loss like Huber) usually gives a more representative fit. MSE is preferable when large errors truly are much worse and the noise is roughly Gaussian.

quickHits.question: Why is cross-entropy used for classification instead of MSE?
quickHits.answer: Cross-entropy directly measures the divergence between predicted probabilities and true labels and heavily penalizes confident wrong predictions, producing strong, well-behaved gradients with sigmoid/softmax outputs. MSE on probabilities leads to weak gradients when predictions are very wrong and slows learning. Matching the loss to the output distribution is the core principle.

quickHits.question: What does it mean if training loss decreases but validation loss increases?
quickHits.answer: That is the classic signature of overfitting: the model is memorizing training data rather than learning generalizable patterns. Responses include early stopping, regularization, more data or augmentation, or reducing model capacity. This is why you always monitor loss on both training and validation sets.

quickHits.question: How does the loss function connect to gradient descent?
quickHits.answer: The loss defines the objective surface; gradient descent computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights and steps in the direction that reduces it. Each update lowers the loss incrementally until convergence at a minimum. In this sense the loss is the feedback signal that drives all learning.

quickHits.question: Is a low loss enough to say a model is good?
quickHits.answer: No. Loss is an optimization target, not a full evaluation; you also need task metrics like accuracy, precision/recall, AUC, or business KPIs, evaluated on held-out data. Class imbalance can make loss misleading, and a model can achieve low average loss while failing on important segments. Use loss for training, proper metrics for judging.

sourceText: Loss Functions: measuring error, guiding learning. A loss function quantifies how wrong predictions are; training minimizes it. Pipeline: compare prediction with true value, quantify error as a number, aggregate (average) over examples, use loss to update parameters. Regression losses: MSE (penalizes larger errors more, sensitive to outliers) and MAE (treats errors linearly, robust to outliers). Classification losses: Binary Cross-Entropy / log loss for binary problems, -[y log(p)+(1-y)log(1-p)]; Categorical Cross-Entropy for multi-class one-hot labels. Cross-entropy heavily penalizes confident wrong predictions. Quick guide: continuous values (price, height) -> MSE/MAE; spam/not spam -> binary cross-entropy; cat/dog/bird -> categorical cross-entropy; recommendation scores -> MSE/MAE. Outliers: MSE dominated by huge squared errors; MAE has linear impact. Loss drives learning: high loss -> compute loss -> update weights via gradient descent -> lower loss. Best practices: pick the loss matching problem and output, understand its penalty shape, monitor train AND validation loss, watch for overfitting (train loss down, val loss up), use proper evaluation metrics beyond loss. Mistakes: wrong loss for the problem, ignoring class imbalance, only watching training loss. Memory: Error -> Feedback -> Learning. Loss guides learning.

title: Chi-Square Test
subtitle: Do observed counts match what we expect?
summary: Explains the chi-square test for categorical count data: comparing observed versus expected frequencies to judge whether differences are due to chance. Covers the test statistic, goodness-of-fit versus independence tests, degrees of freedom, p-value interpretation, assumptions like expected counts above 5, and common mistakes such as using it on numerical data or inferring causation.

concepts.name: When to Use Chi-Square
concepts.summary: Use for categorical count data to compare observed versus expected frequencies or to test whether two categorical variables are related; not for means, numerical data, or small expected counts.
keyPoints: Counts, not means or percentages
Goodness-of-fit or independence
Not valid for expected counts < 5
Use t-test/ANOVA for numerical data

concepts.name: The Chi-Square Statistic
concepts.summary: Chi-square sums (O - E)^2 / E across categories; bigger observed-expected gaps produce a larger statistic and stronger evidence against the null.
keyPoints: x2 = sum((O - E)^2 / E)
O = observed count, E = expected count
Right-skewed distribution, reject in upper tail

concepts.name: Goodness-of-Fit vs Independence
concepts.summary: Goodness-of-fit checks whether one variable's counts fit a hypothesized distribution; the independence test checks whether two categorical variables are associated in a contingency table.
keyPoints: GoF: df = k - 1
Independence: df = (r-1)(c-1)
Both use the same x2 statistic

concepts.name: Factors Affecting the Result
concepts.summary: The result depends on the size of O-E differences, total sample size, magnitude of expected counts, and number of categories.
keyPoints: Larger N gives more power, tiny effects can become significant
Expected counts should be >= 5 (else Fisher's exact)
Many categories dilute power via extra df

concepts.name: Interpreting the P-Value
concepts.summary: The p-value measures how surprising the data would be under the null hypothesis, not the size or importance of the effect.
keyPoints: p < 0.05 = common significance threshold
Small p != large or important effect
Association != causation

concepts.name: Assumptions Checklist
concepts.summary: Valid chi-square inference requires count data, independent observations, mutually exclusive categories, and sufficiently large expected counts.
keyPoints: Data are frequencies, not percentages
Observations independent
Expected >= 5 in at least 80% of cells

quickHits.question: When is a chi-square test appropriate and when is it not?
quickHits.answer: It is appropriate for categorical count data: testing whether observed counts fit a hypothesized distribution (goodness-of-fit) or whether two categorical variables are independent. It is not appropriate for numerical data or comparing means (use t-tests or ANOVA), for paired categorical data (use McNemar's), or when expected counts fall below about 5, where Fisher's exact test is preferred.

quickHits.question: How is the chi-square statistic computed and interpreted?
quickHits.answer: For each category compute (observed - expected)^2 / expected and sum across categories. Under the null hypothesis the statistic follows a right-skewed chi-square distribution with appropriate degrees of freedom; a value in the upper tail (large gaps between O and E) yields a small p-value and evidence against the null.

quickHits.question: How do you determine degrees of freedom for chi-square tests?
quickHits.answer: For a goodness-of-fit test on one variable, df = k - 1 where k is the number of categories. For a test of independence on an r-by-c contingency table, df = (r - 1)(c - 1). Degrees of freedom set the shape of the reference chi-square distribution and thus the critical value.

quickHits.question: Why can a large sample make a chi-square test misleading?
quickHits.answer: Power grows with N, so with very large samples even trivially small deviations from expected proportions become statistically significant. The p-value tells you the difference is unlikely to be chance, not that it matters practically. Pair the test with effect-size measures like Cramer's V and judge practical relevance.

quickHits.question: What do you do if expected cell counts are too small?
quickHits.answer: The chi-square approximation breaks down when expected counts are below about 5 in more than 20% of cells. Options are to combine sparse categories into broader ones, collect more data, or use an exact method such as Fisher's exact test, which does not rely on the large-sample approximation.

sourceText: Chi-Square Test (x2): do observed counts match what we expect? Tests whether differences between observed and expected frequencies in categorical count data are due to chance. Use for: comparing observed vs expected counts, testing independence between two categorical variables, goodness-of-fit to a hypothesized distribution. Not for: numerical data (use t-test/ANOVA), comparing means, small expected counts (<5), paired/continuous measurements. Statistic: x2 = sum((O-E)^2/E); small O-E gaps -> small x2; big gaps -> large x2 -> more evidence against the null; right-skewed distribution with rejection region in upper tail. Four key factors: size of differences, sample size N (large N = more power, tiny diffs can become significant), expected counts (should be >=5, else combine categories or Fisher's exact test), number of categories k (more df can dilute power). Degrees of freedom: goodness-of-fit df = k-1; independence df = (r-1)(c-1). P-value: small p does NOT measure effect size or importance, only how surprising the data are under H0. Assumptions: counts not percentages, independent observations, expected >=5 in >=80% of categories, mutually exclusive categories. Applications: market research, healthcare outcomes, quality control, surveys. Mistakes: using x2 on numerical data, ignoring expected counts, misreading p-value, inferring causation. Memory: the climb from expected to observed - the higher the climb, the less likely chance explains it.

title: Paired t-Test
subtitle: Did something change? Testing whether the mean difference in paired measurements is zero.
summary: Covers the paired t-test for before/after or matched-pair measurements, where analysis focuses on the per-subject differences rather than the raw scores. Explains the t statistic (mean difference over its standard error), the three knobs that drive the result (effect size, variability, sample size), p-value and confidence-interval interpretation, real-world applications, and mistakes like using an independent t-test on paired data.

concepts.name: Paired vs Independent Data
concepts.summary: Paired data measures the same subjects twice (before/after) or matched pairs, focusing on within-subject change; independent data compares different groups.
keyPoints: Same subjects or matched pairs = paired
Different groups = independent t-test
Pairing removes between-subject variability

concepts.name: Analyze the Differences
concepts.summary: Instead of comparing two score sets, compute the difference for each pair and test whether the average difference is zero.
keyPoints: D = After - Before for each subject
Null hypothesis: mean difference = 0
Positive = increase, negative = decrease

concepts.name: The Paired t-Statistic
concepts.summary: t equals the mean difference divided by its standard error, where SE = s_d / sqrt(n).
keyPoints: t = d-bar / SE
SE = sd of differences / sqrt(n)
Larger |t| = more evidence of change

concepts.name: Three Knobs That Change the Result
concepts.summary: Evidence strength depends on the size of the mean difference, the consistency (variability) of the differences, and the number of pairs.
keyPoints: Bigger mean difference -> smaller p-value
More variability -> less power
More pairs -> smaller SE, more power

concepts.name: Confidence Intervals for the Mean Difference
concepts.summary: A 95% CI around the mean difference shows both the size and the uncertainty of the change; intervals containing zero indicate the data are consistent with no change.
keyPoints: CI includes 0 -> difference unclear
CI well away from 0 -> strong evidence
CI conveys magnitude, not just significance

concepts.name: Assumptions and Alternatives
concepts.summary: Differences should be approximately normally distributed and the outcome continuous; otherwise use Wilcoxon signed-rank or McNemar's test.
keyPoints: Check normality of the differences
Wilcoxon signed-rank for non-normal data
McNemar for paired binary outcomes

quickHits.question: When do you use a paired t-test instead of an independent t-test?
quickHits.answer: Use a paired t-test when the two sets of measurements are naturally linked: the same subjects measured before and after an intervention, matched pairs, or the same users under two conditions. The test analyzes per-pair differences, removing between-subject variability. An independent t-test is for two unrelated groups.

quickHits.question: What is the test statistic for a paired t-test?
quickHits.answer: t = d-bar / (s_d / sqrt(n)), where d-bar is the mean of the pairwise differences, s_d is the standard deviation of those differences, and n is the number of pairs. Under the null hypothesis of zero mean difference, t follows a t-distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom.

quickHits.question: Why does pairing increase statistical power?
quickHits.answer: Pairing removes between-subject variability from the comparison: each subject serves as their own control, so the analysis only has to contend with the variability of the changes themselves. That shrinks the standard error relative to an independent-groups design, making real effects easier to detect with the same sample size.

quickHits.question: What does a small p-value in a paired t-test actually tell you?
quickHits.answer: It tells you the observed average change would be unlikely if the true mean difference were zero — evidence against 'no change'. It does not tell you the change is large or practically important. Report the mean difference with a confidence interval to communicate effect size alongside significance.

quickHits.question: What are common mistakes when analyzing paired data?
quickHits.answer: The biggest is running an independent t-test on paired data, which ignores the pairing, discards information, and reduces power. Others include ignoring the direction of changes, not checking that the differences are roughly normal, and over-interpreting p-values as proof of importance. For non-normal differences use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

sourceText: Paired t-Test: 'Did something change?' Tests whether the mean difference in paired measurements is zero. Paired (dependent) data = same subjects measured twice (before vs after) or matched pairs; focus on the change within each subject. Independent data = different groups. Core intuition: compute the difference for each pair (D = After - Before) and test whether the average difference equals zero. Statistic: t = d-bar / SE, SE = s_d / sqrt(n) (s_d = SD of differences, n = number of pairs). Three knobs: (1) mean difference - bigger change, stronger evidence, lower p; (2) variability of differences - more variability lowers power and raises p; (3) sample size - more pairs shrink SE and raise power. P-value scale: 0.5 little evidence, 0.05 common threshold, <0.001 very strong; a small p does NOT mean the change is important, only unlikely due to chance. Confidence intervals: CI including 0 = unclear; CI well away from 0 = strong evidence of real change. Applications: blood pressure before/after treatment, test scores pre/post course, within-subject A/B experiments, measurement reliability. Mistakes: using an independent t-test on paired data (loses power), ignoring direction, not checking that differences are approximately normal, over-interpreting p-values. Alternatives: Wilcoxon signed-rank, McNemar. Remember: look at the changes, not just the scores.

title: RAG + LoRA Support Assistant on Azure
subtitle: Bug ticketing and wiki support system built with RAG and Azure AI Foundry fine-tuning
summary: An end-to-end architecture for an AI support assistant that answers user questions from an internal wiki via RAG and files structured bug tickets when no answer exists. Shows multi-channel intake, Azure orchestration, hybrid vector-plus-keyword retrieval with Azure AI Search, a LoRA fine-tuned GPT-4o model in Azure AI Foundry, and a continuous-learning loop where feedback and resolved tickets become new wiki articles and fine-tuning data.

concepts.name: Multi-Channel Intake and Orchestration
concepts.summary: Users report bugs or ask questions via web portal, in-app chat, email, Teams, or mobile; an API gateway, conversation manager, and intent/severity classifier route each request.
keyPoints: Azure Functions/App Service as API gateway
Azure OpenAI classifies intent and severity
Orchestrator handles logic and routing

concepts.name: Knowledge Retrieval (RAG)
concepts.summary: Queries are embedded with Azure OpenAI embeddings and matched against wiki content using Azure AI Search hybrid (vector + keyword) retrieval, returning top passages with citations.
keyPoints: Hybrid vector + keyword search
Sources: Confluence/SharePoint, Blob docs, Git markdown, internal KBs
Retrieved passages carry citations into the prompt

concepts.name: LoRA Fine-Tuned Assistant
concepts.summary: A GPT-4o/4o-mini model fine-tuned with LoRA in Azure AI Foundry is specialized for support behavior: triage questions, structured tickets, citing wiki evidence, and refusing unsupported answers.
keyPoints: LoRA adapts the base model cheaply
Prefers wiki evidence and cites sources
Refuses to answer without support
Outputs structured ticket format

concepts.name: Prompt Assembly
concepts.summary: A prompt builder combines the system prompt (behaviors and guardrails), conversation history, retrieved evidence, and formatting instructions before generation.
keyPoints: System prompt encodes guardrails
Evidence injected from Azure AI Search
Instructions govern citations, format, tone

concepts.name: Answer-or-Ticket Decision Path
concepts.summary: If the wiki contains an answer, the assistant responds with citations and asks for feedback; if not, it drafts a structured bug ticket (severity, impact, repro steps, environment) into the backlog.
keyPoints: Answer found -> cited response + feedback request
No answer -> ticket with severity, repro steps, affected users
Backlog in Azure DevOps/Jira, prioritized by impact and frequency

concepts.name: Continuous Learning Loop
concepts.summary: Resolutions become draft wiki articles that are reviewed, published, and re-indexed; feedback and high-quality Q&A feed evaluations and new LoRA fine-tuning runs.
keyPoints: Solutions convert to new wiki articles
Re-index updates the knowledge base
Azure AI Foundry evaluations gate new models
Updated model redeployed to the endpoint

quickHits.question: Why combine RAG with fine-tuning instead of choosing one?
quickHits.answer: They solve different problems: RAG grounds answers in current internal knowledge with citations and stays fresh via re-indexing, while LoRA fine-tuning shapes behavior — triage style, structured ticket format, citation discipline, and refusal when evidence is missing. Facts live in the index; skills and tone live in the adapted weights. Together you get trustworthy, current answers delivered in a consistent support workflow.

quickHits.question: What is hybrid search and why use it for retrieval?
quickHits.answer: Hybrid search in Azure AI Search combines vector similarity (semantic matching via embeddings) with keyword/BM25 matching, often fused with reciprocal rank fusion. Vectors catch paraphrases and semantic intent; keywords catch exact identifiers like error codes and product names, which are common in support queries. The combination is more robust than either alone.

quickHits.question: What is LoRA and why use it for this assistant?
quickHits.answer: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes base model weights and trains small low-rank matrices injected into attention layers, adapting behavior at a fraction of full fine-tuning cost. Here it teaches GPT-4o/4o-mini support-specific behaviors: better triage questions, structured tickets, evidence citation, and consistent feedback handling. Adapters are cheap to retrain as new training data accumulates from the feedback loop.

quickHits.question: How does this system prevent hallucinated answers?
quickHits.answer: Multiple layers: retrieval supplies only wiki-grounded passages with citations, the system prompt and fine-tuning both enforce citing sources and refusing unsupported answers, and the decision path routes unanswerable questions into structured bug tickets rather than forcing a response. Feedback ratings and Azure AI Foundry evaluations catch quality regressions before redeployment.

quickHits.question: How does the knowledge base stay current in this design?
quickHits.answer: Unanswered questions become backlog tickets; when engineering resolves them, the solution is drafted into a wiki article, reviewed, published, and the search index is refreshed. This closes the loop so today's unknowns become tomorrow's cited answers, and the same high-quality Q&A pairs feed future LoRA fine-tuning runs.

quickHits.question: How would you measure success for an AI support assistant like this?
quickHits.answer: Track deflection rate (questions resolved without human escalation), answer helpfulness ratings, citation accuracy/groundedness from evaluations, ticket quality (completeness of severity, repro steps), time-to-resolution, and knowledge-base coverage growth. Application Insights dashboards plus Azure AI Foundry evaluations cover both operational and model-quality metrics.

sourceText: Bug Ticketing & Wiki Support System: RAG + Azure AI Foundry (LoRA fine-tuning). (1) User channels: web portal, in-app chat, email, Microsoft Teams, mobile app. (2) Orchestration on Azure: API Gateway (Functions/App Service), Conversation Manager, Intent & Severity Classifier (Azure OpenAI), Orchestrator for logic/routing. (3) Knowledge retrieval: embed query (Azure OpenAI embeddings) -> Azure AI Search hybrid vector+keyword search over wiki sources (Confluence/SharePoint, Blob docs, Git markdown, internal KBs/FAQs) -> top passages with citations. (4) AI Assistant: LoRA fine-tuned GPT-4o/4o-mini in Azure AI Foundry, trained for support behavior - ask better triage questions, structured ticket format, prefer wiki evidence and cite sources, refuse unsupported answers, summarize next steps, convert solutions to wiki articles. Prompt builder combines system prompt (guardrails), history, retrieved evidence, instructions. (5) Answer found in wiki? Yes -> cited answer + feedback request. No -> create bug ticket (severity, impact, repro steps, affected users, environment) into backlog (Azure DevOps/Jira). (6) Prioritization by impact/severity/frequency/business value; engineering resolves; fix drafted as wiki article, reviewed, published, knowledge base re-indexed. (7) Feedback loop: analytics (App Insights), Azure AI Foundry evaluations, training data builder, new LoRA fine-tune, redeploy model. Benefits: cited trustworthy answers, consistent tickets, no knowledge gaps, continuous improvement.

title: REST API
subtitle: How applications communicate over the web
summary: A visual guide to REST APIs using the restaurant-waiter analogy: clients send HTTP requests and servers return responses. Covers request anatomy, HTTP methods and their CRUD mapping, resource-oriented URL design, status code families, query parameters, JSON structure, statelessness, and best practices like using nouns for endpoints and meaningful status codes.

concepts.name: Request/Response Model
concepts.summary: A client (browser or mobile app) sends an HTTP request to a REST API, which processes it (often via a database) and returns an HTTP response — like a waiter carrying orders between customer and kitchen.
keyPoints: Client places the 'order' (request)
Server prepares and returns the response
Communication happens over HTTP

concepts.name: Anatomy of a Request
concepts.summary: A request consists of an HTTP method, an endpoint (resource path), headers such as Authorization and Accept, and an optional body.
keyPoints: e.g. GET /users/42 with Host and Bearer token
Headers carry auth and content negotiation
GET requests have no body

concepts.name: HTTP Methods and CRUD
concepts.summary: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, and DELETE removes — mapping directly to Create, Read, Update, Delete operations.
keyPoints: Create -> POST, Read -> GET
Update -> PUT (replace) / PATCH (partial)
Delete -> DELETE

concepts.name: Resource-Oriented URLs
concepts.summary: REST revolves around resources named with nouns (/users, /users/42, /orders), not action verbs like /getUsers or /createUser; the HTTP method conveys the action.
keyPoints: Nouns for endpoints, methods for actions
URL structure: protocol, host, version, collection, id
Query params handle paging/sorting: ?page=2&limit=25&sort=name

concepts.name: HTTP Status Codes
concepts.summary: Response codes are grouped by family: 2xx success, 4xx client errors, 5xx server errors.
keyPoints: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests
500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable

concepts.name: Statelessness
concepts.summary: Each request is independent and must carry everything the server needs (like auth); the server does not remember previous requests.
keyPoints: Every request re-sends authorization
No server-side session memory in pure REST
Enables horizontal scaling and reliability

quickHits.question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
quickHits.answer: PUT replaces the entire resource with the representation sent — omitted fields are typically reset — and is idempotent. PATCH applies a partial update, changing only the fields provided, such as updating just an email address. Use PUT for full replacement semantics and PATCH for targeted modifications.

quickHits.question: What does it mean that REST is stateless, and why does it matter?
quickHits.answer: Statelessness means the server keeps no memory of prior requests; every request must include all context it needs, such as an Authorization token. This lets any server instance handle any request, which simplifies horizontal scaling, load balancing, and failure recovery. Client state, if needed, lives on the client or in tokens.

quickHits.question: How do HTTP methods map to CRUD operations?
quickHits.answer: POST creates new resources (Create), GET retrieves them (Read), PUT and PATCH update them — full replacement versus partial (Update) — and DELETE removes them (Delete). The method carries the action while the URL names the resource, e.g. POST /users creates a user and DELETE /users/42 removes one.

quickHits.question: What status code would you return for a successful creation, and for a deleted resource?
quickHits.answer: Return 201 Created when POST successfully creates a resource, ideally with a Location header pointing to it. A successful DELETE commonly returns 204 No Content since there is no body to send. Generally: 2xx means success, 4xx means the client made a bad request, and 5xx means the server failed.

quickHits.question: What makes a URL design 'RESTful'?
quickHits.answer: RESTful URLs name resources with plural nouns (/users, /orders, /products) and use path segments for identity (/users/42), letting HTTP methods express the action. Verb-style endpoints like /getUsers or /createUser are less RESTful because they duplicate what the method already says. Versioning (/v1) and query parameters for pagination, filtering, and sorting complete the structure.

sourceText: REST API: how applications communicate over the web. Analogy: API is a waiter — client places an order (HTTP request), server prepares the response, waiter delivers it back. Request anatomy: method + endpoint (GET /users/42), headers (Host, Authorization: Bearer, Accept: application/json), optional body. HTTP methods: GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH partial update, DELETE remove. CRUD mapping: Create->POST, Read->GET, Update->PUT/PATCH, Delete->DELETE. Example calls: GET /users/42 -> 200 OK with user JSON; POST /users -> 201 Created; PATCH /users/42 -> 200 OK; DELETE /users/42 -> 204 No Content. Resources: use nouns (/users, /users/42, /orders); /getUsers, /createUser are less RESTful. Status codes: 2xx success (200, 201, 204); 4xx client errors (400, 401, 403, 404, 429); 5xx server errors (500, 503). URL structure: https:// protocol, api.example.com host, /v1 version, /users collection, /42 resource. Query parameters: GET /users?page=2&limit=25&sort=name. JSON data format: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans. Stateless design: server does not remember previous requests; each request carries authorization. Typical flow: user clicks save -> POST /tasks -> API validates -> DB stores -> 201 Created -> frontend updates UI. Best practices: nouns for endpoints, correct methods, meaningful status codes, consistent JSON.

title: Training vs. Inference
subtitle: Two stages of an ML model's life
summary: Contrasts the two stages of a machine learning model's life: training, where the model learns parameters from labeled data via optimization, and inference, where the fixed trained model makes fast predictions on new, unseen data. Highlights that training is compute-heavy and offline while inference is lightweight and online, and that each stage should be optimized for different goals — accuracy versus speed and scale.

concepts.name: Training (Learning Phase)
concepts.summary: The model starts with random weights and adjusts them via an optimization process to minimize loss on labeled examples, learning patterns and relationships.
keyPoints: Requires labeled data (input + correct output)
Parameters are updated iteratively
Computationally expensive, often on GPUs/TPUs
Typically happens offline

concepts.name: Inference (Prediction Phase)
concepts.summary: The trained model with fixed weights receives new, unlabeled input and produces a prediction that drives a decision or action.
keyPoints: No parameter updates — weights frozen
Input has no label; the model predicts it
Fast and lightweight
Happens online in production

concepts.name: Goals Differ by Stage
concepts.summary: Training aims to learn the best parameters that minimize error; inference aims to generate accurate predictions quickly and reliably at scale.
keyPoints: Optimize training for accuracy
Optimize inference for speed and scale
Good training leads to accurate inference

concepts.name: From Prediction to Action
concepts.summary: Inference output feeds downstream use: predictions become decisions, actions, and automation — this is where the model delivers business value.
keyPoints: Prediction -> decision -> action
Training builds knowledge, inference delivers value
Enables automation in production systems

concepts.name: Operational and Security Considerations
concepts.summary: Training and inference run in different environments with different risks: training data must be kept secure, and production inference systems must be protected.
keyPoints: Training: secure the data pipeline
Inference: protect production endpoints
Different infrastructure profiles (batch GPUs vs serving)

quickHits.question: What is the difference between training and inference?
quickHits.answer: Training is the learning phase: the model sees labeled data and iteratively updates its weights via optimization to minimize loss. Inference is the prediction phase: the trained model's weights are frozen and it maps new, unseen inputs to predictions. Training is compute-heavy and offline; inference is lightweight and runs online in production.

quickHits.question: Why is training so much more computationally expensive than inference?
quickHits.answer: Training requires many passes over large datasets, and each step involves a forward pass, a backward pass to compute gradients, and weight updates — often repeated for millions of iterations on GPUs/TPUs. Inference is a single forward pass per request with no gradient computation or weight updates, so it can be orders of magnitude cheaper per example.

quickHits.question: What do you optimize for in inference that you don't during training?
quickHits.answer: Inference is optimized for latency, throughput, cost, and reliability at scale, since it serves live traffic. Techniques include quantization, pruning, distillation, batching, caching, and specialized serving hardware. Training, by contrast, is optimized primarily for final model accuracy and convergence speed.

quickHits.question: Are model weights updated during inference?
quickHits.answer: No — during inference the weights are fixed; the model only computes a forward pass to produce a prediction. Learning from new data requires a separate retraining or fine-tuning step, after which an updated model is redeployed. This separation keeps serving fast, reproducible, and safe.

quickHits.question: Why does the training/inference split matter for system design?
quickHits.answer: The two stages have different infrastructure profiles: training runs offline in batch on GPU/TPU clusters with access to sensitive labeled data, while inference runs online with strict latency SLOs and public-facing attack surface. Designing them separately lets you scale, secure, and cost-optimize each independently — and remember that training builds knowledge but inference is where the model delivers value.

sourceText: Training vs. Inference: two stages of an ML model's life. Training learns patterns from data and builds the model; inference uses the learned model to make predictions on new data. Training (learning phase): labeled examples (input + correct output) -> untrained model with random weights -> learning process (optimization) adjusts weights to minimize loss -> trained model that has learned patterns and relationships. Goal: learn the best parameters (weights & biases) that minimize error on training data. Key points: data is seen by the model, parameters are updated, computationally expensive, happens offline (often on GPUs/TPUs). Inference (prediction phase): new unseen input (no label) -> trained model with fixed weights (no learning) -> prediction -> use prediction for decision, output, action, automation. Goal: generate accurate predictions quickly and reliably on new data. Key points: new data passed to the model, no parameter updates, fast and lightweight, happens online in production. Why it matters: training builds knowledge, inference delivers value; good training leads to accurate inference. Optimize training for accuracy; optimize inference for speed & scale. Keep training data secure; protect inference systems in production.
